content: The investigators included both prospective and retrospective cohort studies that had a concurrent control group. Population-representative cross-sectional cohorts, as well as nested case-control studies within these cohorts, were also included if the data on outcomes and exposures were collected uniformly through retrospective history recall. However, other types of case-control studies, studies without a control group, and systematic or narrative reviews were excluded. Studies published from the inception of the databases up to the search date were considered, regardless of the language of publication or publication status. For studies published in languages other than English or Hindi, Google Translate was used for translation into English. If the translation raised questions, professional translation into English was commissioned. The participants included young children aged 12–23 months who had been breastfed for at least the first nine months or had a minimum mean/median breastfeeding duration of nine months (if reported as summary statistics) or a minimum range of 6–12 months (if reported as a range). Their mothers were also included. The intervention or exposure of interest was continued breastfeeding during the second year of life (beyond 12 months of age) or a minimum mean/median duration of 15 months (if reported as summary statistics). The comparison group consisted of children who were not breastfed beyond 12 months but had been breastfed for at least the first nine months. If breastfeeding duration was reported only as summary statistics, a minimum mean/median duration of nine months was used for the comparison group. If reported as a range, a minimum of 6–12 months was used. When data were presented separately for breastfeeding durations of 9–12 months and 6–9 months (or 6–12 months), the 9–12 months data were preferred for the comparison group. Studies with simultaneous co-interventions, such as health education or micronutrient supplementation, were included only if the primary difference between the intervention/exposure and comparison groups was the duration of breastfeeding. The search strategy for the main databases is detailed in Appendix 2. Additional resources, such as reference lists of included papers and relevant reviews, were scanned to identify potentially missed citations. Authors of relevant reviews and studies identified during the primary search were contacted for information on other relevant studies. For data collection and analysis, the titles and abstracts of identified studies were independently screened by two authors to exclude irrelevant literature. Full-text articles of the remaining studies were assessed against eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus among all authors. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, including details on methods, participants, settings, interventions, outcomes, and results. Study authors were contacted for clarification or missing data when necessary. Extracted data were independently evaluated by another author, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The risk of bias in included studies was assessed independently by two authors using the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions criteria. For randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials, the criteria included sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, and selective outcome reporting. Each domain was judged as low, high, or unclear risk of bias. For observational studies, the Risk of Bias for Nutrition Observational Studies (RoB-NObs) tool was used, which is a modified version of the ROBINS-I tool tailored for food, nutrition, and public health studies. Potential confounders, such as maternal age, education, socioeconomic status, pre-pregnancy BMI, and infant characteristics, were identified and accounted for in the quality assessment. Measures of treatment effect included risk ratios (RR) or odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for binary outcomes. Continuous outcomes were analyzed using mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) if measured with similar but not identical instruments. Data at the end of the study period were preferred over baseline changes. For observational studies with various breastfeeding durations, adjusted or unadjusted estimates (OR, MD, SMD) were calculated using statistical equations. Cluster-randomized trials were analyzed using cluster-adjusted RR and CI, or adjustments were made using external sources if necessary. Missing data were addressed by contacting study authors or imputing values with the help of a statistician when feasible. Assumptions for imputations were recorded and presented with the results. Heterogeneity was assessed for variability in participants, interventions, and outcomes to identify clinical and methodological diversity. A random-effects model was used for meta-analysis unless the populations and settings differed significantly, in which case a narrative synthesis was provided. Subgroup analyses were performed for child development and growth outcomes, such as IQ, underweight, and obesity, based on breastfeeding duration, study population development status, area of residence, and year of publication. Sensitivity analyses were conducted concerning risk of bias parameters. The search identified 19,214 studies after removing duplicates from 33,193 records. A total of 170 records from 146 studies were included, while 415 records were excluded after full-text review. Among the included studies, 93 provided data on child outcomes, and 54 on maternal outcomes, with one study reporting both. Child outcomes included development, growth, obesity, cardiometabolic outcomes, infections, iron deficiency/anemia, bone health, oral health, and asthma/atopy. Maternal outcomes included cancer, cardiometabolic parameters, bone health, anthropometry, cognitive impairment, and diabetes. Reasons for exclusion of studies are detailed in the Characteristics of Excluded Studies section, with the most common reason being the lack of evaluation of continued breastfeeding beyond one year.
